title: Beginner question: choosing a tile size (16x16 or 48x48)

posts.author: LuxInterior
posts.body:
Hi everyone!
Just bought Mz and am a total noob. I’ve been doing some searching, but can’t find a simple answer about choosing a tile size (48x48 or 16x16).
I’m mostly a musician and writer - visual art is not my forte. So I was really happy when I found so much great pixel art on itchio. I’m looking for a style that’s simpler and blockier than the default rtp assets, (more snes style) and found a ton of stuff I like.
But most of it is in 16x16. And when I try making stuff with that setting, it seems to throw things off - like I’ll try to lower the overall resolution, but then the window is tiny and weird.
I know people say that rpg maker is meant to work a certain way, and if you try to break out of that, it’ll fight you every step of the way. Is it better to just do everything at 48 pixels, and upscale most of the assets? Or is it worth fiddling around to get things good at 16 pixels, so I can just plug most of the assets in?
Thanks so much! Looking forward to being active on these forums.

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
I think the easiest way to work with 16x16 is to set the editor to be using 32x32 and just scale up all of the tilesets by 100%.
They'll look pixelated ("simpler and blockier") and it won't screw with the UI/camera as badly.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
MZ was originally made for 48x48, the other size options were added later on user demand.
the biggest problem with the lower resolution grid (either 16x16 or 32x32) is the fact that the menues require a minimum screen size by default - which basically means you'll have to use plugins to change the menu for smaller sizes.
@ATT_Turan
mixed up a bit above - the resize from 16 to 32 is 200%, not 100%.
And if you go from 16x16 upscale it doesn't matter if you use 200% to go to 32 or 300% to go to 48.
You only get problems if you are at a base of 32 and try to upscale by 150% to 48, because resizing by partial sizes will always cause either distortion or blurring and quality loss.

Scaling is easy.
When it come to character sprites, as long as all the frames are the exact same size, you'll be fine.
And being a good artist, is nothing but a lot of practice. Your first own set may look like a monkey humped your mouse, but that is fine. Your 10th set will look decent and your 100th set will look damn fine. And believe me, I know, you want damn fine straight away... But you got to make the monkey humping  the keyboard stuff first, or it won't happen.
There is no pill that makes any of us a good artist, although... There are some things that improve your performance... And not all of those are expensive or illegal. Vitamine D is very effective, and can be obtained just by taking a walk in the sunshine. Coffee also helps, although if you live in the US, you probably classify starbucks as coffee, in which case it isn't a healthy option at all.
But since you will use upscaled 16x16 graphics, I have a more serious tip for you: When you make your own graphics in that format, draw them first, scale them up  to 48x48 (300%) after. If you edit them, scale them back down to 16x16 (66.67%), then edit them, and then scale them back up to 48x48. That way you don't have to worry about pixels lining up and be all 3x3 in size.
